title: Paul and Barnabas split (Acts 15:36–41)
hookLine: a sharp disagreement over young Mark; later Paul calls Mark useful
tomorrow: Paul dreams of a man in Macedonia. who's waiting when he lands?
last: SEEMED GOOD TO THE HOLY SPIRIT.

lines: WHO GETS A SEAT IN THE CAR?
cards: Planning a road trip is the easy part. The fight starts over who gets a seat in the car. Antioch, not long after the council.

Paul says to Barnabas: "Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do." Barnabas is in, and he wants to bring young John Mark. Paul says no.
Not him. Not the one who left last time. Two friends who stood side by side in front of crowds and councils are now standing face to face, and neither one is backing down.

teach.b: Paul's reason is right there in the text. Mark is the one "who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work."

Barnabas, whose name Acts once explained as "The son of consolation," wants to give him another chance. A later letter calls Mark "sister's son to Barnabas," so this is family, too. Both men have a point.
Paul is thinking about the road and the work ahead; Barnabas is thinking about the young man in front of him.
And Acts doesn't tidy it up: "the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other." Barnabas takes Mark and sails for Cyprus. Paul chooses Silas and goes by land.
Acts never says who was right. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight, and it's outside Acts. Letters that carry Paul's name mention Mark later, warmly.
One counts him among Paul's fellow workers.
Another says: "Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry." Tradition takes him to be the same Mark.
If so, the young man Paul wouldn't travel with became the one he asked for by name. The split was real. So, it seems, was the mending.

how: Some readers set this story beside Colossians 4:10 and 2 Timothy 4:11, where Mark appears again near Paul; tradition holds that it is the same Mark.

games.q: what does “paul and barnabas split” mean?
o: a sharp falling-out between two friends over Mark
a church dividing into two denominations
a quarrel over whether Gentiles needed the law

p: went not with them to the work

s: holy people in the Bible never fall out with each other
Acts calls this contention so sharp that they departed asunder.
Acts says Paul was right about Mark
Acts never picks a side. each man goes, with a partner.
a later letter has Paul asking for Mark by name
take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me.

games.q: two friends of yours on the yearbook staff fall out over a deadline and quit the same project. each one asks you who was right. what fits today's story?
o: don't crown a winner; keep a door open to both.
side with the one who's usually more reliable.
get them in one room tonight and settle it for good.
games.why: Acts never says who was right. and the mending, if the letters are a guide, came later, not that night.

practice: Grab a pen and any scrap of paper. Write the first name of someone you parted from badly, and beside it one word you'd still wish them: peace, rest, luck, anything true.
Nothing needs sending or fixing; if you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Paul and Barnabas split. A sharp disagreement over John Mark, and two journeys instead of one.

orig.note: Greek: a sharp contention, the word in Acts 15:39.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: they parted, and later mended, and Paul asked for Mark by name. Go gently.
